prompt.en: A mountain club can reach a hilltop repeater on VHF, but two valley stations cannot hear each other directly. Which propagation limit best explains the valley-to-valley problem?

text.en: The VHF path is mostly line-of-sight and the terrain blocks it.
The D region is absorbing all VHF ground wave.
The signal must wait for F2 multi-hop propagation.
The skip zone always begins at the transmitting antenna.

explanation.en: Ordinary VHF communication depends strongly on antenna height and clear paths. A repeater on high ground may see both stations even when they cannot see each other.

prompt.en: An HF antenna is adjusted so more energy leaves at a steep upward angle. What coverage goal does that favour when the ionosphere supports it?

text.en: A longer first skip distance than a low-angle signal

explanation.en: High-angle HF radiation is the idea behind NVIS: it returns relatively nearby compared with low-angle long-distance radiation.

prompt.en: Two HF signals use the same ionospheric region. One leaves the antenna at a shallower angle. What happens to its first return point?

text.en: It becomes a ground wave instead of a sky wave.
It returns at the same distance because power sets skip distance.
It reaches farther away before returning.
It stops being affected by ionization.

explanation.en: With similar layer height, a shallower launch angle produces a longer geometric path before the wave returns to Earth.
